SEC. 6. Criminal Penalties.
SEC. 6.1. Section 6814.1 is added to the
Corporations Code, to read:
6814.1. Every director, officer or agent of any clinic
subject to Section 12586.3 of the Government Code
who either knowingly misreports expenditures or
revenues under Section 12586.3 of the Government
Code or knowingly participates in a scheme to route
expenditures or revenues through related parties as
defined in Section 12586.3 of the Government Code,
including, but not limited to, related foundations, with
intent to artificially increase their Mission Spend Ratio,
is punishable by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision
(h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code, or by
imprisonment in a county jail for not more than one
year.
SEC. 7. Severability.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any provision
of this act or its application is held invalid, that invalidity
shall not affect other provisions or applications that can
be given effect without the invalid provision or
application.
SEC. 8. Effective Date.
Consistent with the purposes of this act, the
requirements on Mission Spend Ratio provided by this
act shall apply to each clinic’s first full fiscal year
beginning at least 6 months after passage of this act.
SEC. 9. Amendment.
Pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 10 of Article II of
the California Constitution, this act may be amended
either by a subsequent measure submitted to a vote of
the people at a statewide election; or by statute validly
passed by the Legislature and signed by the Governor,
but only to further the purposes of this act.
SEC. 10. Competing Measures.
In the event this measure and another measure that
governs Mission Spend Ratio at some or all covered
clinics appear on the same statewide ballot, the
provisions of the other measure or measures shall be
deemed to be in conflict with this measure. Another

CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,

STUDYOFPOTENTIALIMPACTSFROMTHECLINIC FUNDINGACCOUNTABILITYANDTRANSPARENCYACT 3
Executive Summary
This study summarizes the methodology, underlying data, and results of our analyses of federally qualified
health centers (FQHCs) and FQHC Look-Alikes in California. We have assessed the financial operations and
services provided at FQHCs and other clinics and calculated the financial impact that the proposed ballot
measure “Attorney General Initiative 25-0008A1” (Ballot Measure)1 will have on FQHCs and FQHC Look-
Alikes in California as well as its effects on the state’s healthcare landscape. This analysis specifically
focused on the Ballot Measure’s proposed requirement that clinics spend at least 90% of their revenue on
program expenses. Importantly, the Ballot Measure’s calculation of what can be included in the 90% ratio
excludes critical mission related and patient care related expenses. Further, the Ballot Measure requires
clinics that fall below the 90% spending threshold to pay an annual penalty equal to the amount that
would bring a clinic into compliance with the 90% threshold. Clinics will also pay a registration fee that is
meant to cover state expenses related to enforcing the spending requirement and administrative efforts
to process, evaluate, and disseminate collected data.2 We have outlined our key findings below.
• An investigation into the financial situation of FQHCs and Look-Alikes in California details a
challenging financial picture, one with the potential to be made significantly worse if clinics incur
anticipated penalties from the Ballot Measure.
• Most of the clinic parent organizations (91% or 183 of 202) analyzed do not meet the initiative’s
arbitrary 90% spend ratio requirement.
• Those organizations could pay $1.7 billion in total penalties in the first year alone – money from
the clinics that would be redirected from patient and mission related expenses into a state penalty
fund. Clinics would face similarly crippling penalties every year.
• The overwhelming majority of the organizations (88% or 161 out of 183) will have a total negative
margin as a result of this measure – putting clinics at risk of closure.
• Organizations at risk of closing were associated with between 1.3 million and 11.7 million patient
encounters in 2023 – including up to 7.7 million encounters from Medi-Cal patients.
• The strict 90% ratio would not allow clinics to keep funding in reserves for major capital
investments, such as opening new clinics, purchasing new equipment or technologies,
investments into value-based care, and preparing for potential public health or other
emergencies.
• The Initiative will increase State General Fund costs by more than $1 billion, primarily because
displaced patients will be forced to receive care in more costly settings, including county and
University of California clinics, and hospital emergency rooms.

Background
Community health clinics (CHCs), typically non-profits, provide a variety of medical and community
services, especially primary care services, in an outpatient clinic setting regardless of a person’s ability to
pay.3 By serving patients with no health insurance, limited financial means, or living in underserved
geographic areas, these clinics provide a vulnerable segment of the population with preventive and
essential medical care, with the hope of reducing more extreme and expensive medical interventions. The
Ballot Measure focuses on FQHCs and FQHC Look-Alikes. FQHCs must adhere to stricter regulatory
requirements compared to other clinics due to one of their primary sources of income, federal grants from
the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) under Section 330 of the Public Health Service
(PHS) Act (42 U.S.C. § 254b).4 When a clinic receives this funding, it agrees to specific financial, compliance,
and reporting requirements meant to ensure that clinics operate efficiently and effectively. FQHCs also
receive funding from Medicare and Medi-Cal and agree to additional oversight intended to ensure that
“costs are reasonable, necessary, and directly related to patient care” (42 CFR § 413.9).5 FQHC Look-Alikes
meet all of the eligibility requirements of an FQHC but do not receive HRSA grant funding.
The United Healthcare Workers (UHW) union, part of the larger Service Employees International Union
(SEIU), filed the Ballot Measure with the hope of qualifying for the 2026 November election. This Measure
imposes strict and arbitrary spending requirements on FQHCs and Look-Alikes, with a penalty for any clinic
that does not meet this requirement.
An investigation into the financial situation of FQHCs and Look-Alikes in California details a challenging
financial picture, one with the potential to be made significantly worse if clinics incur anticipated penalties
from the Ballot Measure. The Ballot Measure requires that each Clinic report a “Spend Ratio”, which is
calculated as the “total amount spent on activities that accomplish each clinic’s exempt purposes divided
by that clinic’s total revenue.” If a clinic does not meet a 90% threshold on the Spend Ratio, then the clinic
is required to pay a penalty equal to the amount that constitutes the difference between the clinic’s
expenses and the amount that the clinic would need to spend to meet the 90% threshold.6

Summary of Data and Methodology
IRS Form 990 Data
To evaluate the Initiative’s financial impact on FQHCs and Look-Alikes in California, we used organization-
level data sourced from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) form 990s, which is a tax form filed by tax-
exempt organizations, non-exempt charitable trusts, and section 527 political organizations.7 The IRS form
990 data is relevant for this analysis because the Initiative requires that the organization’s Spend Ratio be
calculated using the expenses related to the organization’s “exempt purpose.” The Initiative requires that
clinics use “total program service expenses” from line 4e of Part III and total revenue from line 12 of part
I of form 990. The California Primary Care Association (CPCA) collected form 990 data for 202 organizations
for 2023 and 2024 and provided it to us for analysis. The data shared by CPCA contains revenue and
expense information sourced directly from the form 990s as well as financial metrics derived using form
disclosures. We reviewed and confirmed CPCA’s calculation of these financial metrics, which included the
Spend Ratio, the penalty proposed in the Ballot Measure, and clinics’ operating margin/income. We also
compared the form 990 data to other publicly available data for the same time period, to ensure that the
numbers obtained from the form 990 data were reasonable.
The IRS form 990 is required for most FQHCs and Look-Alikes but has not historically been used to identify
“mission-related” expenditures. Line 4e of Part III of the IRS form 990 does not explicitly include all
expenses that are necessary in order for the clinics to provide vital medical care, such as community
outreach and education, medical devices and technology, state licensing fees, health insurance enrollment
assistance, case management, electronic health record systems, and population health software, to name
a few. Clinics need to incur these expenses to adequately meet the health care needs of the vulnerable
populations it serves. This data was used for this analysis because it was the best available data to estimate
the financial impact of the Measure on clinics in California.
Public HCAI Data
We leveraged the California Department of Health Care Access and Information (HCAI) Primary Care Clinic
data to identify encounter, revenue, and expense data for the 202 organizations in the form 990 data.8 The
HCAI Primary Care Clinic data includes clinic demographic and descriptive information, income statements,
and encounter data. We used this data to assess the Initiative’s potential impact on the California
healthcare marketplace. The HCAI Primary Care Clinic reporting form, data, and documentation is
published by HCAI annually.9

Linking Form 990 and HCAI data
We identified individual clinics from the 2023 HCAI Primary Care Clinic data that are associated with the
organizations that submit IRS form 990 data based on the clinic and parent organization names in the HCAI
data and the parent organization names in the IRS form 990. Of the 202 organizations identified in the IRS
form 990 data, we identified all but six (6) organizations in the HCAI Primary Care Clinic data. In addition,
we found eight (8) organizations present in the 2023 data that did not submit any information and were
flagged in the data as “non-responsive”.10,11 The 188 organizations that reported data in 2023 relate to 782
individual clinics in the HCAI Primary Care Clinic data. Of these 782 clinics found, 727 (93%) are classified
as FQHCs or FQHC Look-Alikes. These 727 clinics represent 90% of all clinics in the 2023 HCAI Primary Care
Clinic data that are classified as FQHCs or FQHC Look-Alikes.
Summary of Analyses Performed
We used the IRS form 990 data and HCAI Primary Care Clinic data to complete the analyses outlined below
and measure the potential effects of the proposed Ballot Measure.12
We sought to determine the impact on clinics by first identifying the number of organizations that would
be out of compliance with the Initiative’s 90 percent Spend Ratio requirement. We also calculated the
penalties that would be assessed on clinics that did not meet the Spend Ratio requirement. Using that
information, we determined the financial impact that the Initiative would have on clinics’ balance sheet,
and their ability to operate. We identified three (3) scenarios in which clinics would potentially close due
to the financial burden that the penalties and the overall Initiative would impose on them.
We evaluated the additional impact on the healthcare market in California by identifying the number of
encounters, by payer, that would be displaced in the event of clinic closures using the three (3) scenarios
in which clinics would potentially close. We also determined the challenges posed to the California
healthcare system due to this financial strain and loss of important healthcare infrastructure.
Then, we estimated the fiscal impact on the State. First, we isolated the impact and additional costs that
California would incur due to the administration of the provisions. We identified provisions that require
increases in the State’s bureaucracy, provisions that impose penalties on clinics, and provisions that will
increase the costs for other General Fund-supported programs, thereby widening the General Fund deficit.
We then enumerated the indirect effect on state General Fund revenues and expenditures.

Determine the Impact on Clinics
Spend Ratio and Clinic Compliance
As defined by the Initiative, an organization’s Spend Ratio is the total amount spent on activities that
accomplish each organization’s exempt purpose divided by that organization’s total revenue. Using the IRS
form 990 data and language in the Initiative, we calculated the Spend Ratio as an organization’s total
program expenses divided by total revenue. The Initiative requires that organizations have a 90% or
greater Spend Ratio, or they will be subject to penalties to bring them into compliance.
As shown in Exhibit 1, we estimated that 183 (91%) of the 202 organizations in the IRS form 990 data would
not meet the 90% Spend Ratio requirements. When an organization is out of compliance, it will pay a
penalty that reconciles the total program expenses with revenue, so that the total program expenses plus
the penalty divided by the revenue is equal to 90%.13 We estimated that organizations will be asked to pay
$1.7 billion in penalties in just the first year. While the Initiative indicates that the penalties will go to the
administration of the program, along with funding for workforce training, recruitment, and retention, it is
unlikely that all the organizations will be able to pay the penalty. The assessment of $1.7 billion in penalties
in the first year alone will have significant implications for clinic operations.14

Prop 44: The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Prop 44: The Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Why We Need Prop 44
Every year, billions in taxpayer dollars go to Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs)—our local community clinics—to provide high-quality, affordable healthcare for low-income and underserved communities.
Unfortunately, some clinic executives have lost sight of that mission:
Overpaid Executives: Millions of dollars intended for patients are going toward bloated executive salaries and non-essential spending.
Less Than 50% Spent on Care: Some community clinics spend less than half of their revenue on direct healthcare services.
$1.7 Billion Misdirected: An estimated $1.7 billion currently floating through the clinic system is not being spent on core patient care.
At a time when healthcare facilities face massive federal funding cuts, healthcare dollars must go where they belong: to patient care and the caregivers on the front lines.
What Prop 44 Will Do
Prop 44 will require Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), also known as community clinics, to spend a minimum of 90% of their revenues on caregivers, patient care, and furthering their mission of care. That means taxpayer money is going where it truly belongs: to direct care and the caregivers who provide it.
How will Prop 44 work
If a clinic fails to meet the 90% goal (which means they spent more than 10% of revenues on executive pay or other non-essentials) they will be fined. The money from the fines will go into an escrow account that they can earn back if they meet the 90% threshold in future years. This encourages clinics to do the right thing and makes sure funds that can be used for patient care are not lost.
Can clinics afford this? Will it hurt clinics?
Some community clinics are already meeting this goal, which shows others can do it too. But too many clinics are wasting money on executive pay and non-essentials: there is an estimated $1.7 billion in the clinics system that is not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop 44 will make sure that healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good. That will improve clinics, not hurt them.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Support

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> It applies to federally qualified health centers, community clinics that deliver primary care to underserved populations. There are about 2,000 such safety-net clinics in California, run by either private nonprofits (in most cases) or public entities like counties, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026).
Proposition 44 would require these clinics spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on patient care. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent. Some of this money could be earned back if clinics come into compliance. There would be criminal penalties for knowingly misreporting or misclassifying expenses to get around the limits.
Advertisement
The text of the measure specifies only that 90% of revenue must be used for “program services advancing their charitable purpose” and does not spell out which expenditures would qualify as program-related and which would not. The task of determining which expenses fall on what side of the ledger would belong to the state attorney general.
The state Department of Public Health would be permitted to temporarily waive a clinic’s spending requirements in exceptional circumstances.

Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents workers in the healthcare industry. SEIU-UHW West is the primary backer of Californians for Responsible Healthcare and the Yes on 44 (https://yesonprop44.com/) campaign.
Supporters say the measure would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses at clinics serving the state’s most vulnerable residents.

Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Organizations publicly opposing Proposition 44 include the California Medical Assn., the California Hospital Assn., which represents hospitals and health systems, the Assn. of California Healthcare Districts, which represents the state’s 76 public healthcare districts, the California Teachers Assn., the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliate, the state Democratic Party, the state Chamber of Commerce and Reform California, a conservative advocacy group.
Opponents say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted in the 90% of revenues, prompting clinics to cut programs to avoid financial penalties. A study (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation alone, an additional expense that could leave up to 88% of clinics operating in the red.
Opponents also say the measure adds an expensive layer of bureaucracy to the state’s budget and grants elected officials — in this case, the attorney general — authority to determine which services clinics can offer.
What will it cost?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> If the proposition passes, enforcement will cost the state “in the low tens of millions of dollars” annually, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The measure requires clinics to pay annual fees to cover enforcement costs. The proposition also could incur additional costs for state and local governments depending on the attorney general’s interpretation of what constitutes program expenses.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 is one of two measures put forth by SEIU-UHW this election cycle, along with Proposition 40, better known as the billionaire tax.

Supporters say the measures will shore up California’s healthcare funding in the face of federal cuts. Opponents say they ultimately will cost far more than they add to state coffers and are on the ballot as a result of SEIU-UHW’s oft-repeated strategy of using ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) as a negotiating tactic.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a social worker says Proposition 44 will ensure funding actually reaches patients. The opposing view: A physician argues that the measure’s poor design will end up hurting (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-44-destructive-community-clinics/) the vast majority of clinics. Guest Commentary written by Sandra Carranza Sandra Carranza is a social worker at a community clinic in San Diego. California’s community clinics are meant to help patients when they need care the most. That’s why I chose to go into healthcare. For more than 20 years, I’ve worked in San Diego helping families get the care they need. Too often, what I see inside our clinics doesn’t align with the mission. The funding doesn’t reach the front lines of patient care, and it’s patients who lose out. Every day I see people facing barriers to receiving the care they need. Many wait months for an appointment. Others can’t afford their medications, or give up on treatment when an insurance change makes it more expensive. As a healthcare worker, I support Proposition 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act. Prop. 44 simply requires community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. It holds clinics accountable for the public dollars they receive, and it lets patients and taxpayers finally see where the money goes. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Proposition 44 wrongly squeezes politics between California patients and their healthcare (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-44-destructive-community-clinics/) It doesn’t limit what clinics can spend on patient care — it does the opposite. Rather than cutting the services patients depend on, it makes sure the funding reaches them. People come to us because they trust we’ll be there when they need us. We owe it to them to have the staff, equipment and resources to care for them the way they deserve. That responsibility is never more urgent than in an emergency. I’ve been in the room when a patient needed a defibrillator, the device that shocks a stopped heart back into rhythm, and the staff scrambled to find one that actually worked. In a cardiac emergency, every second matters. A patient’s life should never depend on whether we can find working equipment in time. Community clinics receive billions in healthcare dollars to care for the people who need it most. But some spend as little as half of their funding on actual patient care, while the rest goes to bloated executive salaries and other costs that have nothing to do with the patient in front of us. When the equipment healthcare workers need isn’t there in an emergency, that’s the money I think about. California could lose $30 billion in annual healthcare funding thanks to cuts from Congress (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/). Clinics across our state are already closing (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-grant-hospital-closures/), and coverage is slipping away for more than a million Californians. Every remaining dollar has to reach patients. This matters to me personally. My sister has cerebral palsy, and because my mother didn’t speak English, I was translating for my family by the time I was 6 years old so my sister could get the care she needed. For families like mine, interpretation and language access weren’t extras, they were how we got care. Under Prop. 44, funding for those services would be protected. Prop. 44 doesn’t take a dollar away from community clinics. It keeps the funding where it is and makes sure it goes where it belongs: to patients. At a moment when California is losing so much, accountability matters more than ever. I hope the people who run our clinics remember why they chose this work in the first place. Healthcare isn’t about excessive executive salaries or impressive new buildings. It’s about the patient sitting in front of us, trusting that we’ll be there when they need us. That’s the standard our community clinics should live up to, and it’s the standard every patient deserves. Proposition 44 ensures California’s community clinics prioritize patients over executives

By Sandra Carranza, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a social worker says Proposition 44 will ensure funding actually reaches patients. The opposing view: A physician argues that the measure's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics.

Guest Commentary written by

California's community clinics are meant to help patients when they need care the most. That's why I chose to go into healthcare. For more than 20 years, I've worked in San Diego helping families get the care they need.

Too often, what I see inside our clinics doesn't align with the mission. The funding doesn't reach the front lines of patient care, and it's patients who lose out.

Every day I see people facing barriers to receiving the care they need. Many wait months for an appointment. Others can't afford their medications, or give up on treatment when an insurance change makes it more expensive.

As a healthcare worker, I support Proposition 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act. Prop. 44 simply requires community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. 

It holds clinics accountable for the public dollars they receive, and it lets patients and taxpayers finally see where the money goes.

It doesn't limit what clinics can spend on patient care — it does the opposite. Rather than cutting the services patients depend on, it makes sure the funding reaches them. People come to us because they trust we'll be there when they need us. We owe it to them to have the staff, equipment and resources to care for them the way they deserve.

That responsibility is never more urgent than in an emergency. I've been in the room when a patient needed a defibrillator, the device that shocks a stopped heart back into rhythm, and the staff scrambled to find one that actually worked. In a cardiac emergency, every second matters. A patient’s life should never depend on whether we can find working equipment in time.

Community clinics receive billions in healthcare dollars to care for the people who need it most. But some spend as little as half of their funding on actual patient care, while the rest goes to bloated executive salaries and other costs that have nothing to do with the patient in front of us.

When the equipment healthcare workers need isn't there in an emergency, that's the money I think about.

California could lose $30 billion in annual healthcare funding thanks to cuts from Congress. Clinics across our state are already closing, and coverage is slipping away for more than a million Californians. Every remaining dollar has to reach patients.

This matters to me personally. My sister has cerebral palsy, and because my mother didn't speak English, I was translating for my family by the time I was 6 years old so my sister could get the care she needed. For families like mine, interpretation and language access weren't extras, they were how we got care.

Proposition 44 wrongly squeezes politics between California patients and their healthcare

By Brent Sugimoto, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a physician argues that Proposition 44's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics. The opposing view: A social worker says the measure will ensure funding actually reaches patients.

Guest Commentary written by

Primary care doctors train for patients at every stage of life, from children to older adults, to provide the lifelong, comprehensive medical care that millions of Californians rely on. Improving the health of all residents is our mission.

Many of us are worried about Proposition 44 this November and are urging voters to reject it.

Family physicians work at community health clinics throughout the state, providing essential care for millions of patients. Prop. 44 would put that care at risk.

How?

The measure sets strict spending requirements for nonprofit health clinics that could put billions of dollars in revenue at risk, creating arbitrary standards that an estimated 91% of health centers don’t meet. A study commissioned by the California Primary Care Association found that clinics could pay as much as $1.7 billion in penalties the first year alone, with more to follow every year. That’s essential funding that keeps facilities open and helps community health clinics offer the whole-person, whole-community care they are known for.

Upending health center budgets like this could have devastating consequences. It would push the vast majority of clinics across California into the red, forcing facilities to make impossible choices about which services to eliminate.

Unless Prop. 44 is defeated, many clinics that offer safety-net care could even close.

California's community health clinics serve more than 7 million patients each year, including children, working families, the uninsured, seniors, veterans and 1 in 3 Medi-Cal patients. Prop. 44 threatens the resources these clinics rely on.

The measure is terribly drafted and rife with legal flaws that are going to wind up saddling clinics with enormous financial penalties — just for spending resources on the important staff and patient services that keep clinics running and Californians connected to care. Under Prop. 44, clinics would be financially penalized for investments like capital projects, new equipment and technology upgrades, disaster prep or even if they put revenue in its budget reserves.

Anyone who has worked in or relied on a community health clinic knows that healthcare does not end in an exam room. Ensuring that patients have access to transportation, telemedicine when they cannot make it to the clinic, and healthcare enrollment navigators to help them sign up for the health insurance they qualify for are all essential components of keeping people healthy.

Prop. 44 puts far too much on the line.

While all of these provisions are worrisome, perhaps most concerning is that Prop. 44 squeezes a politician between a patient and their clinic. The measure essentially puts the state’s Attorney General — an elected official with no healthcare experience — in charge of decisions about which services health clinics can and cannot provide.

If we’ve learned anything over the last several years, it’s that politicians should stay out of the relationship between providers and patients.

Our healthcare system is already under enormous strain. Costs are already too high, patients are already waiting too long to see a doctor or a specialist, and emergency rooms are already overcrowded.

If the effects of Prop. 44 force clinics to close and patients to lose access to care, their health needs do not disappear. Patients will delay treatment and end up in hospital emergency rooms for routine care, resulting in more emergency room overcrowding, longer wait times and higher healthcare costs.

It’s not just primary care doctors — the opposition to this measure is vast and bipartisan. Millions of patients across the state are counting on our votes.

Endorsement: Prop 44 uses California’s most vulnerable patients as cannon fodder
Prop 44 would establish strict spending requirements for a subset of nonprofit clinics — and, in so doing, undermine patient care.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 19, 2026
On its surface, everything about Proposition 44 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on California’s November ballot looks appealing.
Its title is straightforward (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm): “Requires community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services.”
And the text of the measure boldly declares its intent to “ensure clinic patient service delivery and workforce stability is prioritized over management and overhead spending.”

Great. After all, these clinics, which are largely funded by taxpayers (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106815), provide low-cost or free care to uninsured and low-income residents in disadvantaged neighborhoods. Given the huge looming federal cuts to healthcare, why wouldn’t Californians vote to ensure limited dollars are spent on services for vulnerable patients, rather than administrative bloat or padding executives’ salaries?
Well, because Prop 44 will almost certainly make things worse for patient care.
The details are wonky, but you don’t have to dig deep to spot the farce.
Prop 44 would establish strict spending requirements for a subset of community health clinics known as “federally qualified health centers” run by private nonprofits that are already subject to extensive federal regulations (https://bphc.hrsa.gov/compliance/compliance-manual). The measure would mandate these clinics spend at least 90% of their revenue on things related to their nonprofit “mission” — i.e., patient care — and a maximum of 10% on management and administrative expenses, including fundraising.

“We are just trying to ensure that when these federal health cuts really hit, that these clinics are ready and that they can stay open and operational for the people who need them,” rather than “spending money on extravagant fundraisers, on excessive executive pay,” Renée Saldaña, press secretary of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union that put the measure on the ballot, told the editorial board.
Yet Prop 44 creates a complex administrative and legal regime that will drain limited staff time and resources from these nonprofit clinics while distracting from patient care.
Under the measure, clinics that fail to meet the 90% ratio — which most currently don’t, (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250392.pdf) according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office — will be fined the difference and ordered to pay the state Department of Public Health within 30 days. These fines and other fees will then be used to pay for the state’s enforcement of the measure — at a cost, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated, of tens of millions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026) of dollars annually.
Clinics can lobby to get the money back by proving their compliance with the measure within five years. If they can’t comply, the state would use remaining penalty funds for programs supporting “clinical worker training, recruitment and retention.” To get a temporary waiver from Prop 44’s requirements, clinics would have to prove “unexpected or exceptional circumstances.”

That’s tens of millions siphoned from the most vulnerable patients in the state — right when they can least afford it with President Donald Trump’s healthcare cuts.
All this red tape is in service of solving a problem that arguably doesn’t exist.
Most clinics in California already appear to be using their funds responsibly. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf), clinics report spending an average of about 80% of their revenue on healthcare services.
Where did the measure’s 90% benchmark come from? Was it born from industry best practices? Have other states used similar regulatory regimes to improve clinic outcomes?
No. Prop 44’s proponents made it up.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Declan Walsh, a senior analyst for the union, told us that Prop 44 was partially modeled on New Mexico’s medical loss ratio program, which requires insurance companies to spend 90% of their premiums on medical claims rather than administrative tasks.
That comparison, however, makes little sense. For-profit insurance companies don’t operate like nonprofit safety-net health clinics; for starters, insurers can invest premiums to boost revenue. (Those investment returns don’t count against the 90% cap (https://www.hsd.state.nm.us/wp-content/uploads/Turquoise-Care-MCO-Model-Contract-CLEAN_Final.pdf) in New Mexico.)
Meanwhile, administrative costs — like records management, human resource departments and office supplies — are necessary to keep clinics up and running.
Nor would Prop 44 necessarily curtail the type of spending that the union wants to limit.
Saldaña, for example, lamented the fact that AltaMed, which operates more than 60 community clinics in Southern California, “spent almost half a million dollars moving art from Europe in 2023.”

Article continues below this ad
That number isn’t quite accurate — federal documents show (https://www.foundationsearch.com/990/LATEST/9H/ALTAMED%20HEALTH%20SERVICES%20CORP%202022%20952810095.HTML) AltaMed spent about $266,000 to purchase art from Europe in fiscal year 2022. AltaMed classified this spending as “program services” for “art as a holistic approach to healthcare.”
But that is seemingly permissible under Internal Revenue Service guidelines — which Prop 44 does not change. The IRS gives nonprofits considerable discretion in categorizing spending; it defines “program services” (https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i990#en_US_2025_publink11283jd0e12335) as “mainly those activities that further the organization’s exempt purposes” and notes this can encompass everything from lobbying governments to publishing magazines.
We agree with the union that some of those categories could be tightened to prevent abuses. Just last month, a watchdog group asked the IRS to investigate AltaMed (https://campaignforaccountability.org/watchdog-requests-irs-investigation-into-altamed-health-services-corp-for-potential-private-inurement-or-excess-benefit-transaction-violations/) for questionable spending that appears to disproportionately benefit the CEO and his family.
But Prop 44 wouldn’t meaningfully address those issues — that would require federal reform.
The measure does permit the California attorney general to “issue binding guidance” on how clinics can define “total program service expenses” and “total revenue,” but it’s unclear how that might interact with federal law.
And any tweaks to the IRS framework are bound to trigger legal battles, especially given the measure’s high stakes: It explicitly notes that any “director, officer or agent” of a clinic that knowingly misreports expenditures or revenues could face incarceration.
Amid this murky mess, Prop 44 could cause clinics to close (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop44-110326.pdf).
Julia Liou, CEO of Asian Health Services, told us that she estimated Prop 44 could cost her Bay Area clinics, which serve more than 50,000 vulnerable residents, about $11 million a year — an impact even more devastating than that of the federal cuts.
Dozens of community health clinics and respected healthcare organizations — including the California Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics-California and the California Hospital Association — are opposed to the measure (https://noprop44.com/our-coalition/), citing its potential to irreversibly damage a critical component of the healthcare safety net.
So why is Prop 44 on the ballot, given that it will likely end up harming the very patients it claims to want to protect?
Because the measure’s sponsor, SEIU-UHW, and its leader, Dave Regan, have a long history of cynically leveraging marginalized Californians as bargaining chips.
This is the same union that sent California voters three ballot measures in six years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-dialysis-prop-29-17408398.php) to tighten staffing regulations at kidney dialysis clinics, all of which voters overwhelmingly rejected. The measures purported to be about protecting patient health but were transparently aimed at forcing the unionization of dialysis clinic workers.
According to reporting in Politico (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/07/a-grand-canyon-sort-of-disagreement-how-clinics-and-a-union-leader-sparred-over-prop-44-00988013), Regan told Francisco Silva, head of the California Primary Care Association, which represents many community clinics, that he would drop Prop 44 if Silva agreed to let Regan unionize 25,000 clinic workers. (Regan denies this.)

Regan, who’s also behind Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, has been shameless in trying to get his way.As the Chronicle recently reported (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/seiu-dave-regan-billionaire-tax-22427506.php), an independent investigation substantiated allegations from other union leaders that Regan had attempted to “extort” support for the billionaire tax and bullied and threatened those who questioned the measure’s effectiveness.

California’s Proposition 44: Potential big impacts for community health centers
Oct 29, 2026
Share LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=)X (Twitter) (https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=)Email (mailto:?body=) Copy URL
If approved, the measure would impose new spending, reporting, penalty, and governance rules on covered federally qualified health centers and look-alikes.
What's the impact?
If approved by voters in November, Prop. 44 would impose mandatory spending, reporting, penalty, and liability requirements on covered federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) and look-alikes.
Covered clinics would need to meet a 90% mission spend ratio (MSR) or risk administrative penalties tied to total revenue.
Clinics, boards, lenders, and partners should assess how Prop. 44 could affect operations, governance, reserves, and contracts.

Federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) are a key part of California's primary care safety net. Against a backdrop of ongoing concerns over healthcare affordability and access, California voters will consider Proposition 44 (Prop. 44) on the November ballot. If approved, Prop. 44 would establish new spending, reporting, enforcement, and governance requirements for covered FQHCs and FQHC look-alikes.
The authors of Prop. 44, also called the "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf)" claim that some clinics allocate too much revenue to executive pay, administration, and surpluses rather than patient care. In response, the measure would establish a 90% mission spend ratio (MSR) for covered entities, meaning FQHCs would need to use at least 90% of their revenue for patient care. The law would also create enforcement mechanisms for noncompliance, including administrative penalties, potential private lawsuits by patients, and possible criminal liability for clinic leaders.
This article summarizes the parties supporting and opposing Prop. 44, what the measure would do, and the questions health centers, their boards, and their lenders and partners should be asking now to prepare themselves for what may come should Prop. 44 be approved.
Behind the scenes: Who supports and who opposes Prop. 44?
Prop. 44 is backed primarily by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, a statewide labor union representing more than 120,000 healthcare workers in some of California's largest private-sector hospitals and clinics. Proponents argue that Prop. 44 would increase accountability for how covered clinics use their revenue and would direct penalty funds toward workforce recruitment, training, and retention.
Several healthcare professional associations and over 150 organizations oppose the measure, arguing that Prop. 44 will make it unnecessarily difficult for clinics to operate in California, artificially restrict how clinics spend and invest their funding, and make healthcare delivery more burdensome.
Who is covered
Prop. 44 applies to California clinic corporations that are FQHCs under the federal Medicaid statute and FQHC look-alikes-organizations designated by the federal Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) as meeting health center program requirements without receiving a Section 330 grant. Because Prop. 44's coverage is based on federal status rather than size, the measure would apply to both large multi-site systems and small rural clinics. Tribal and urban Indian organizations, however, would be excluded from Prop. 44's reach.
The Mission Spend Ratio
Prop. 44's central mechanism is its proposed MSR, which is calculated by dividing a clinic's total spending on its exempt purpose divided by its total revenue. Both figures start from the clinic's IRS Form 990: "total program service expenses" as the numerator and "total revenue" as the denominator.
But the Form 990 is only the starting point. Prop. 44 would allow the California Attorney General to verify clinics' reported figures and "binding guidance" on how to calculate the MSR that could impact what counts as "program service expenses" or "total revenue." As a result, the figures used to calculate a clinic's MSR could differ from the amount reported on its Form 990.
This framework raises several practical considerations. First, if the attorney general issues guidance affecting how figures are defined or calculated, clinics may not be able to determine their MSR from audited financials alone. Second, because the MSR uses revenue as the denominator, rather than expenses, certain financial practices-such as maintaining operating reserves or spending a capital grant over several years-could affect whether a clinic meets the 90% threshold. Third, because Prop. 44 would allow the attorney general to issue guidance through bulletins or notices without formal rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act, standards for calculating the MSR could change without public notice and comment.
The penalty and the escrow account
CALCULATING THE PENALTY
Failure to meet the 90% threshold would have considerable consequences. Under Prop. 44, a clinic with an MSR below 90% would owe an administrative penalty equal to the difference between its mission spending and 90% of total revenue.
The measure would require the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) to assess the penalty within 30 days of receiving the attorney general's calculation. For example, a clinic reporting $50 million in revenue and $40 million in mission spending would have an MSR of 80%, triggering a $5 million penalty-the difference between its mission spending and 90% of total revenue.
One important consideration for clinics is that the penalty methodology is not capped and does not depend on a finding of fault or patient harm. As a result, clinics will face potentially significant penalties even if they deliver quality care to their patients.
HOLDING PENALTY FUNDS IN ESCROW
Prop. 44 would also establish two potential avenues for relief for clinics. First, the measure would allow clinics to recover any penalties they paid so long as (1) the clinic reaches its 90% MSR goal and (2) the clinic secures an agreement with CDPH dictating how the refunded monies will be spent on mission-directed expenses. Although the refund mechanism suggests that clinics may retain an interest in previously paid penalties, Prop. 44 would also allow CDPH to use penalty funds to cover costs associated with administering the MSR program. As a result, the funds a clinic seeks to recover could be diminished by the time the necessary conditions are met to satisfy conditions of repayment.
Under Prop. 44, a clinic could also seek a one-year waiver from the MSR penalty system, but they'd be required to demonstrate unexpected or exceptional circumstances or doubt about the clinic's ability to continue operation. The measure, however, does not include any confidentiality protections for these waiver filings, so a waiver request-including information like financial records, hardship statements, or disclosures about the clinic's ability to continue as a going concern-would be available through the California Public Records Act, potentially exposing the clinic to a different kind of risk.
As a result, Prop. 44's penalty and waiver provisions could subject clinics to a loss of property without judicial review or determination of forfeiture and require them to disclose private information that would otherwise be kept confidential.
Reporting, fees, audits, civil liability, and criminal exposure
In addition to administrative penalties, Prop. 44 could also create a risk of exposure to civil and criminal liability. Under the measure, clinics would be required to file annual data with the attorney general's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers and pay an additional annual fee. Late filers would face fines of $5,000 for a first violation, followed by an additional $10,000 for each month a report is late. The attorney general would also have authority to audit clinics, their contractors, and related parties.
Prop. 44 would also change nonprofit governance law by allowing any patient of a clinic that fails to report, or that falls below 90% without a waiver, to sue that clinic to remedy a "breach of a charitable trust." In those suits, Prop. 44 would provide that good faith is not a defense and that the business judgment rule does not apply. This is significant because the business judgment rule presumes that corporate directors make informed decisions in good faith and in the best interest of the organization, even if the consequences of a certain action turn out badly. If passed, Prop. 44 would deny covered clinics' directors the benefit of these protections. The measure would also allow private parties to file lawsuits against clinics under the State's Unfair Competition Law.
Prop. 44 would also expose directors, officers, and agents who knowingly misreport figures, or who route revenue or spending through related parties to inflate the ratio, to possible criminal prosecution, conviction, and even imprisonment.
Altogether, Prop. 44 would expand potential civil and criminal exposure for clinics and their leaders by broadening who may file suit and increasing the risk of misdemeanor or felony prosecution.
Why this matters
Most FQHC revenue comes from the Medi-Cal and Medicare prospective payment system (PPS) rates and federal Health Center Program funds, each governed by federal law. Because the proposed MSR penalty is calculated against total revenue, Prop. 44 could effectively capture federally guaranteed payment and federally restricted program income for state purposes if approved.
This potential use of federally appropriated funds raises federal preemption questions. The measure's approach also resembles percentage-based charity regulations the US Supreme Court has rejected under the First Amendment. Furthermore, because the MSR penalty is uncapped and not tied to fault, it may also raise concerns under the federal and state Excessive Fines Clauses. These issues could provide grounds for legal challenges if Prop. 44 is approved. However, the measure's severability clause (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop44-text-proposed-laws.pdf) could allow portions of Prop. 44 to remain in effect even if other provisions are challenged or invalidated.
Nixon Peabody's Healthcare team will be closely watching developments around Prop. 44 and its potential impact on FQHCs, boards, lenders, and partners. For more information on the content of this alert, please contact your Nixon Peabody attorney or the authors of this alert.

Proposition 44 pits California clinics against union known for ballot battles
By Ben Paviour
September 17, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The healthcare union behind a proposed California billionaire tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317240033.html) has a second, less-talked-about ballot measure with a different target: health clinics.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West’s Proposition 44 would require nonprofit, federally funded clinics that care for underserved populations to spend 90% of their revenues on services that advance their mission. If they don’t comply, they would face fines that would be returned to them if they hit the 90% spending target within five years.
The union argues that clinics are investing their revenue poorly, wasting it on everything from art to executive compensation of up to $1.9 million a year.
But its more numerous critics argue the measure represents an existential crisis for the clinics it purports to save. They say Prop. 44 is the latest in a series of ballot battles waged by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan that’s really aimed at creating leverage over employers in labor negotiations.
The backdrop for the fight is H.R. 1, the mixture of tax cuts and a Medicaid overhaul signed by President Donald Trump last year. That bill is expected to cause 2 million Californians to lose health insurance (https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/over-two-million-more-californians-projected-to-lack-health-insurance-by-2030/) by 2030, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center.
SEIU-UHW argues that Prop. 44 will strengthen clinics by making them more accountable, while its critics say it will weaken them at a time of acute need.
While SEIU-UHW insists it will put resources behind the measure, the union hasn’t invested any major funds in Prop. 44 since May, instead funneling its dollars to support the billionaire tax. Opponents of the measure, meanwhile, had $32 million in cash on hand as of the end of June and have continued to raise money since then.
The proposition is one of the least popular of the 14 statewide measures on this year’s ballot, according to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html). Just 34% of the 1,745 California adults surveyed said they backed it.
Registered nurses Hope Wallen and John Bergmann rally against the cuts to Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, outside Rep. Kevin Kiley’s district office in Rocklin on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. The cuts are part of legislation in Congress known as President Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, which had passed the Senate earlier in the day and must now return to the House. HECTOR AMEZCUA hamezcua@sacbee.com
What clinics pass the Prop. 44 benchmark?
At its heart, Prop. 44 centers on tax returns that every nonprofit files with the federal government.
Clinics and other nonprofits are required to report how much revenue they make and how much they spend on program services. Prop. 44 uses that number as the baseline for its calculation of “mission spend ratio.” The California attorney general could modify what is or isn’t included on that list that would count toward the 90% spending on program services.
Brad Fulton, head of Indiana University’s Philanthropy Research Hub who is not involved in the fight, assessed the potential impact of Prop. 44 at the request of The Sacramento Bee using their tax returns.
Fulton found that 89% of the 147 California clinic organizations (many of which operate multiple clinics) would fail to meet Prop. 44’s spending threshold and face $1.6 billion in first year fines. Of the 16 organizations that did meet it, all but two had finances in the red, suggesting they are financially distressed. Fulton argued the proposition effectively would limit clinics from accumulating surpluses and reserves.
“Almost no health center in the U.S. meets Prop. 44’s standard,” Fulton wrote.
California Primary Care Association President Francisco Silva said clinics anticipated the growing need for their services, pointing to the effects of HR 1.
“This is the time to actually grow health centers so we can serve that patient base, not to cut them back,” Silva said in an interview.
Both the Democratic and Republican state parties formally adopted a “no” stance on Prop. 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html). Other organizations opposed to the measure include Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the California Teachers Association and the California Chamber of Commerce.
The only group to endorse Prop. 44 beyond its sponsor is the California Federation of Labor.
Spokesperson Renée Saldaña said she expected more organizations to join the coalition. She said the measure is designed to hold taxpayer-funded clinics to a higher standard.
“We want to cut what we see as wasteful spending and redirect that money so that patients can access this care when they need it,” Saldaña said in an interview.
The fight behind the fight
Prop. 44 wound up on the ballot after a breakdown in negotiations between Regan, the SEIU-UHW president, and Silva’s California Primary Care Association.
Silva said those negotiations centered on unionization efforts at clinics rather than the clinic spending at the center of Prop. 44 — proof, he contends, of Regan’s true intentions with the measure.
SEIU-UHW has often filed ballot measures for organizations that have resisted its unionization efforts, including a series of recent measures that would have placed new regulations on dialysis clinics.
SEIU-UHW healthcare workers protest layoffs, relocations and wage proposals outside Kaiser Permanente on Wednesday May 2, 2018 in Sacramento. Paul Kitagaki Jr. pkitagaki@sacbee.com
The union has increasingly turned its attention to clinics, some of which are already unionized.
It initially sought to pass a version of Prop. 44 through the Legislature. Its 2025 bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1113), which failed to pass, would have exempted clinics that set up “labor-management cooperation committees” from the 90% threshold.
“The emergency is here now,” Saldaña said. “Clinics are already closing and so we took it directly to the voters.”
Some clinics that would be affected by Prop. 44 have fought unionization efforts. For example, Innercare, which operates more than a dozen health and dental clinics across the state, spent more than $577,000 on a consulting firm that aimed to discourage workers from joining the union in 2024, according to federal filings.
The National Labor Relations Board is currently considering allegations that Innercare illegally harassed and terminated employees during the 2024 unionization drive. SEIU-UHW alleges that Innercare retaliated against pro-union workers, offered perks to anti-union workers and engaged in unlawful surveillance.
Innercare Executive Vice President Young Kwon said in a statement that more than 60% of the workers voted against joining the union and that the company is “committed to fostering a respectful, lawful and supportive workplace.”
“Innercare denies that it engaged in unlawful conduct or violated employees’ rights under federal labor law in any way,” Kwon said.
Prop. 44 critics like Silva those fights shouldn’t be lumped together with the ballot measure, which wouldn’t change anything about clinic unionization.
“It’s an accusation to distract from what’s really in front of the voters,” he said.

The initiative defines this as the *mission-spend ratio*, which would be calculated annually by the California Attorney General.

Proposition 44 ensures California’s community clinics prioritize patients over executives

By Sandra Carranza, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a social worker says Proposition 44 will ensure funding actually reaches patients. The opposing view: A physician argues that the measure's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics.

Guest Commentary written by

California's community clinics are meant to help patients when they need care the most. That's why I chose to go into healthcare. For more than 20 years, I've worked in San Diego helping families get the care they need.

Too often, what I see inside our clinics doesn't align with the mission. The funding doesn't reach the front lines of patient care, and it's patients who lose out.

Every day I see people facing barriers to receiving the care they need. Many wait months for an appointment. Others can't afford their medications, or give up on treatment when an insurance change makes it more expensive.

As a healthcare worker, I support Proposition 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act. Prop. 44 simply requires community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. 

It holds clinics accountable for the public dollars they receive, and it lets patients and taxpayers finally see where the money goes.

It doesn't limit what clinics can spend on patient care — it does the opposite. Rather than cutting the services patients depend on, it makes sure the funding reaches them. People come to us because they trust we'll be there when they need us. We owe it to them to have the staff, equipment and resources to care for them the way they deserve.

That responsibility is never more urgent than in an emergency. I've been in the room when a patient needed a defibrillator, the device that shocks a stopped heart back into rhythm, and the staff scrambled to find one that actually worked. In a cardiac emergency, every second matters. A patient’s life should never depend on whether we can find working equipment in time.

Community clinics receive billions in healthcare dollars to care for the people who need it most. But some spend as little as half of their funding on actual patient care, while the rest goes to bloated executive salaries and other costs that have nothing to do with the patient in front of us.

When the equipment healthcare workers need isn't there in an emergency, that's the money I think about.

California could lose $30 billion in annual healthcare funding thanks to cuts from Congress. Clinics across our state are already closing, and coverage is slipping away for more than a million Californians. Every remaining dollar has to reach patients.

This matters to me personally. My sister has cerebral palsy, and because my mother didn't speak English, I was translating for my family by the time I was 6 years old so my sister could get the care she needed. For families like mine, interpretation and language access weren't extras, they were how we got care.

Proposition 44 ensures California’s community clinics prioritize patients over executives

By Sandra Carranza, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a social worker says Proposition 44 will ensure funding actually reaches patients. The opposing view: A physician argues that the measure's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics.

Guest Commentary written by

California's community clinics are meant to help patients when they need care the most. That's why I chose to go into healthcare. For more than 20 years, I've worked in San Diego helping families get the care they need.

Too often, what I see inside our clinics doesn't align with the mission. The funding doesn't reach the front lines of patient care, and it's patients who lose out.

Every day I see people facing barriers to receiving the care they need. Many wait months for an appointment. Others can't afford their medications, or give up on treatment when an insurance change makes it more expensive.

As a healthcare worker, I support Proposition 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act. Prop. 44 simply requires community clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. No more than 10% can go to executive pay, administration and overhead. 

It holds clinics accountable for the public dollars they receive, and it lets patients and taxpayers finally see where the money goes.

It doesn't limit what clinics can spend on patient care — it does the opposite. Rather than cutting the services patients depend on, it makes sure the funding reaches them. People come to us because they trust we'll be there when they need us. We owe it to them to have the staff, equipment and resources to care for them the way they deserve.

That responsibility is never more urgent than in an emergency. I've been in the room when a patient needed a defibrillator, the device that shocks a stopped heart back into rhythm, and the staff scrambled to find one that actually worked. In a cardiac emergency, every second matters. A patient’s life should never depend on whether we can find working equipment in time.

Community clinics receive billions in healthcare dollars to care for the people who need it most. But some spend as little as half of their funding on actual patient care, while the rest goes to bloated executive salaries and other costs that have nothing to do with the patient in front of us.

When the equipment healthcare workers need isn't there in an emergency, that's the money I think about.

California could lose $30 billion in annual healthcare funding thanks to cuts from Congress. Clinics across our state are already closing, and coverage is slipping away for more than a million Californians. Every remaining dollar has to reach patients.

This matters to me personally. My sister has cerebral palsy, and because my mother didn't speak English, I was translating for my family by the time I was 6 years old so my sister could get the care she needed. For families like mine, interpretation and language access weren't extras, they were how we got care.

Proposition 44 wrongly squeezes politics between California patients and their healthcare

By Brent Sugimoto, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a physician argues that Proposition 44's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics. The opposing view: A social worker says the measure will ensure funding actually reaches patients.

Guest Commentary written by

Primary care doctors train for patients at every stage of life, from children to older adults, to provide the lifelong, comprehensive medical care that millions of Californians rely on. Improving the health of all residents is our mission.

Many of us are worried about Proposition 44 this November and are urging voters to reject it.

Family physicians work at community health clinics throughout the state, providing essential care for millions of patients. Prop. 44 would put that care at risk.

How?

The measure sets strict spending requirements for nonprofit health clinics that could put billions of dollars in revenue at risk, creating arbitrary standards that an estimated 91% of health centers don’t meet. A study commissioned by the California Primary Care Association found that clinics could pay as much as $1.7 billion in penalties the first year alone, with more to follow every year. That’s essential funding that keeps facilities open and helps community health clinics offer the whole-person, whole-community care they are known for.

Upending health center budgets like this could have devastating consequences. It would push the vast majority of clinics across California into the red, forcing facilities to make impossible choices about which services to eliminate.

Unless Prop. 44 is defeated, many clinics that offer safety-net care could even close.

California's community health clinics serve more than 7 million patients each year, including children, working families, the uninsured, seniors, veterans and 1 in 3 Medi-Cal patients. Prop. 44 threatens the resources these clinics rely on.

The measure is terribly drafted and rife with legal flaws that are going to wind up saddling clinics with enormous financial penalties — just for spending resources on the important staff and patient services that keep clinics running and Californians connected to care. Under Prop. 44, clinics would be financially penalized for investments like capital projects, new equipment and technology upgrades, disaster prep or even if they put revenue in its budget reserves.

Anyone who has worked in or relied on a community health clinic knows that healthcare does not end in an exam room. Ensuring that patients have access to transportation, telemedicine when they cannot make it to the clinic, and healthcare enrollment navigators to help them sign up for the health insurance they qualify for are all essential components of keeping people healthy.

Prop. 44 puts far too much on the line.

While all of these provisions are worrisome, perhaps most concerning is that Prop. 44 squeezes a politician between a patient and their clinic. The measure essentially puts the state’s Attorney General — an elected official with no healthcare experience — in charge of decisions about which services health clinics can and cannot provide.

If we’ve learned anything over the last several years, it’s that politicians should stay out of the relationship between providers and patients.

Our healthcare system is already under enormous strain. Costs are already too high, patients are already waiting too long to see a doctor or a specialist, and emergency rooms are already overcrowded.

If the effects of Prop. 44 force clinics to close and patients to lose access to care, their health needs do not disappear. Patients will delay treatment and end up in hospital emergency rooms for routine care, resulting in more emergency room overcrowding, longer wait times and higher healthcare costs.

It’s not just primary care doctors — the opposition to this measure is vast and bipartisan. Millions of patients across the state are counting on our votes.

Proposition 44 wrongly squeezes politics between California patients and their healthcare

By Brent Sugimoto, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will decide this fall if community clinics should be required to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and whether to empower the state Attorney General to settle disputes. Below, a physician argues that Proposition 44's poor design will end up hurting the vast majority of clinics. The opposing view: A social worker says the measure will ensure funding actually reaches patients.

Guest Commentary written by

Primary care doctors train for patients at every stage of life, from children to older adults, to provide the lifelong, comprehensive medical care that millions of Californians rely on. Improving the health of all residents is our mission.

Many of us are worried about Proposition 44 this November and are urging voters to reject it.

Family physicians work at community health clinics throughout the state, providing essential care for millions of patients. Prop. 44 would put that care at risk.

How?

The measure sets strict spending requirements for nonprofit health clinics that could put billions of dollars in revenue at risk, creating arbitrary standards that an estimated 91% of health centers don’t meet. A study commissioned by the California Primary Care Association found that clinics could pay as much as $1.7 billion in penalties the first year alone, with more to follow every year. That’s essential funding that keeps facilities open and helps community health clinics offer the whole-person, whole-community care they are known for.

Upending health center budgets like this could have devastating consequences. It would push the vast majority of clinics across California into the red, forcing facilities to make impossible choices about which services to eliminate.

Unless Prop. 44 is defeated, many clinics that offer safety-net care could even close.

California's community health clinics serve more than 7 million patients each year, including children, working families, the uninsured, seniors, veterans and 1 in 3 Medi-Cal patients. Prop. 44 threatens the resources these clinics rely on.

The measure is terribly drafted and rife with legal flaws that are going to wind up saddling clinics with enormous financial penalties — just for spending resources on the important staff and patient services that keep clinics running and Californians connected to care. Under Prop. 44, clinics would be financially penalized for investments like capital projects, new equipment and technology upgrades, disaster prep or even if they put revenue in its budget reserves.

Anyone who has worked in or relied on a community health clinic knows that healthcare does not end in an exam room. Ensuring that patients have access to transportation, telemedicine when they cannot make it to the clinic, and healthcare enrollment navigators to help them sign up for the health insurance they qualify for are all essential components of keeping people healthy.

Prop. 44 puts far too much on the line.

While all of these provisions are worrisome, perhaps most concerning is that Prop. 44 squeezes a politician between a patient and their clinic. The measure essentially puts the state’s Attorney General — an elected official with no healthcare experience — in charge of decisions about which services health clinics can and cannot provide.

If we’ve learned anything over the last several years, it’s that politicians should stay out of the relationship between providers and patients.

Our healthcare system is already under enormous strain. Costs are already too high, patients are already waiting too long to see a doctor or a specialist, and emergency rooms are already overcrowded.

If the effects of Prop. 44 force clinics to close and patients to lose access to care, their health needs do not disappear. Patients will delay treatment and end up in hospital emergency rooms for routine care, resulting in more emergency room overcrowding, longer wait times and higher healthcare costs.

It’s not just primary care doctors — the opposition to this measure is vast and bipartisan. Millions of patients across the state are counting on our votes.
